I'm on the AI software development train like everyone else. I can't deny the
productivity boost---it's too dramatic, too undeniable at this point to avoid---but a
whole raft of new challenges is coming along for the ride, and I want to get some of my
early thoughts down.

I'm building a company, so I'm not just making weekend toys for personal use (although
I've done some of that, [too](https://nick-dorsch.github.io/blog/posts/lex/)). My career
and my reputation are on the line, I have skin in the game, so I can't just vibe and
pray that the LLM slot machine keeps delivering what I need to provide value to clients,
I need systems and guiding principles for navigating.

This is doubly true for enterprise grade data systems, which is what I specialize in,
but it applies to any project where your ass is on the line, and the reliable
functioning of the system _actually matters_.

I should state at the outset that I don't have decades of experience to draw from, my
career is 9 years long, and programming has only been a part of that for about 4. I
learn quickly, but I can't claim any special wisdom, either. I'm just trying to navigate
responsibly. From what I've gathered, these challenges seem to be applying to engineers
across a range of different experience levels.

So, for whatever it's worth, I've been mentally noting my internal clench-o-meter for
the last six months while doing different kinds of work, and I've started crystallizing
some thoughts:

## Software engineering and the Blues

> _"It's not the notes you play, it's the notes you don't play"_
>       --- Myles Davis (maybe)

I've played guitar since I was 10.

The thing about learning to play guitar, is that once you can play fast, you spend about
10 years before you finally shut the fuck up.

I shut the fuck up about 3 years ago, and nowadays I play blues, funk, and a bit of jazz
and samba.

With the guitar, your fingers kind of... babble. Certain ergonomic shapes and patterns
are the path of least resistance for your brain, so you end up repeating "licks" a lot.
The problem is that those ergonomic patterns often don't map to sounds that people
actually want to hear.

Freebird is cool, Eddie Van Halen is cool, but sometimes... you know, just... shut the
fuck up.

I think we've all suddenly been given the Devil's hands and become facemelting
shredders, and things are getting _really noisy_.

This will happen outside of software soon, too. It won't be long until the office is
overflowing with the HTML equivalewnt of Freebird at max volume on repeat.

## Where can your system withstand the vibes?
